title: When the origin is not allowed
summary: Why the simplex needs a changed start. A ≥ limit puts the origin outside the region, which the table shows as a negative right-hand side, and the first pivot moves onto the region; minimising by maximising −C; and the two other starts that miss the origin (a lower bound and an equality). A graph beside the table shows each move.

slides.title: When the origin is not allowed

els.text: When the origin is not allowed
Starting the simplex from a ≥ limit or a minimise
Explain why the simplex needs a changed start, and make the change.

•  See why a ≥ limit can make the origin not allowed
•  Use the first pivot to get onto the region
•  Minimise by maximising −C

slides.title: Where the simplex starts
slides.brief: Recap: the earlier deck's problem. The origin is a corner of the region, so the table can start there.

els.text: At the origin, the corner where $x = 0$ and $y = 0$
The origin is in the region, so the table can start there.
This is the problem from the last lesson.

slides.title: Is the origin allowed?
slides.brief: The new limit cuts the origin off. The shaded region is what is allowed.

els.text: A new limit: at least 3 items in total
Test the origin in the new limit:

slides.title: Writing a ≥ limit for the table
slides.brief: The same limit, written the way the table needs it. The right-hand side becomes negative: that is the point of the next slide.

els.text: Writing a ≥ limit for the table
The table only has ≤ limits, so turn it round
Multiplying by $-1$ flips the sign: $\ge$ becomes $\le$.
Now it has a slack variable, like the other two.

slides.title: The table says the same
slides.brief: The start is still x = 0, y = 0, which is exactly why s3 comes out negative.

els.text: $s_3 = -3$: we would have $-3$ left over. That cannot happen.
A negative right-hand side means this start is not allowed.

slides.title: Which entry do we pivot on?
slides.brief: Either negative entry gives a corner of the region here. In general the new right-hand sides must all be positive; if one would be negative, try another entry.

els.text: Which entry do we pivot on?
In the row with the negative right-hand side
Pick a negative entry in this row: the $x$ entry or the $y$ entry. Both are $-1$.
Either works. We take $x$. If a right-hand side would go negative, try the other entry.

slides.title: Moving onto the region
slides.brief: The first pivot's job is only to get onto the region. After it, the algorithm carries on as before.

els.text: Divide the pivot row, then clear the column
Every right-hand side is positive: $x = 3$, $y = 0$, $P = 6$. We are on the region.

slides.title: What did the pivot do?
slides.brief: Why it works: a negative slack is a broken limit; making it zero puts us exactly on the limit's line.

els.text: It took $s_3$ out of the table
Before: $s_3 = -3$. The limit $x + y \ge 3$ was broken.
After: $s_3 = 0$, so $x + y = 3$ exactly. The limit is used up, and we are on its line.
$x$ came in to take its place, along the $x$ axis, until it met the limit at $(3, 0)$.

slides.title: Then carry on as before
slides.brief: The first pivot gets onto the region; the rest is the algorithm from the earlier deck.

els.text: From the region, the usual steps

els.latex: \begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\text{step}&\text{in / out}&\text{corner}&P\\\hline \text{start}&&(0,0) \text{ not allowed}&\\ 1&x \text{ in, } s_3 \text{ out}&(3,0)&6\\ 2&s_3 \text{ in, } s_1 \text{ out}&(5,0)&10\\ 3&y \text{ in, } s_2 \text{ out}&(4,2)&14\end{array}

els.text: After the first pivot: the most negative entry, then the smallest ratio.
Maximum: $P = 14$ at $x = 4$, $y = 2$. The same as before: the new limit was never the one that mattered.

slides.title: Minimising
slides.brief: Minimise C = 3x + 2y on a strip. Check each corner by hand: C is 12, 18, 12 and 8. P = −C turns the smallest C into the largest P.

els.text: Smallest $C$ is the same as largest $-C$
The table maximises, so we give it $P = -C$.
$-8$ is bigger than $-12$ and $-18$. The largest $P$ is the smallest $C$.

slides.title: Minimising: two signals
slides.brief: Minimise C = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≥ 4 and x + y ≤ 6, as maximise P = −C. The bottom row has no negatives at the start, which is the trap.

els.text: Maximise $P = -C$, and look at the table
Bottom row: no negatives, so it says stop.
Right-hand side: $-4$, so it says this start is not allowed.
The right-hand side comes first: we have not got a corner to stop at.

slides.title: The answer, with its sign
slides.brief: Two pivots from the start: (4, 0) with P = −12, then (0, 4) with P = −8. The minimum of C is 8, not −8.

els.latex: \begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\text{step}&\text{in / out}&\text{corner}&P\\\hline 1&x \text{ in, } s_1 \text{ out}&(4,0)&-12\\ 2&y \text{ in, } x \text{ out}&(0,4)&-8\end{array}

els.text: No negatives left in the bottom row: $P = -8$ is the maximum.

slides.title: A lower bound moves the origin
slides.brief: A lower bound y ≥ 1 moves the origin to (0, 1). With Y = y − 1 the origin is allowed again and the problem is in standard form. The optimum is the same point as before, (4, 2), P = 14.

els.text: A lower bound moves the origin

els.latex: \text{Let } Y = y - 1, \text{ so } y = Y + 1 \text{ and } Y \ge 0

els.text: The origin $(x, Y) = (0, 0)$ is allowed: it is $(0, 1)$ on our graph.

slides.title: The new graph starts at 0
slides.brief: The same problem in the new variables: the region is the same shape, with the line y = 1 as the x axis, so the origin is the corner (0, 1) of the old graph. The optimum (4, 1) in (x, Y) is (4, 2) in (x, y).

els.text: $Y = y - 1$: the line $y = 1$ is now $Y = 0$, so it is the new $x$ axis.
The origin $(x, Y) = (0, 0)$ is allowed, so the table can start there.
The best point is $(x, Y) = (4, 1)$, which is $(x, y) = (4, 2)$.

slides.title: An equality: the region is a line
slides.brief: An equality is both a ≤ and a ≥ limit. The region collapses to the line segment inside the other limits, from (2, 3) to (5, 0); P is 13 at (2, 3) and 10 at (5, 0).

els.text: An equality: the region is a line
Say $x + y = 5$ on the earlier problem
A point must be exactly on the line, so write it as two limits:
The $\ge$ limit makes the start negative, so it is handled just as before.
Only the line from $(2, 3)$ to $(5, 0)$ is allowed. Best: $P = 13$ at $(2, 3)$.

•  Maximise? If it is a minimise, use $P = -C$.
•  Every limit ≤? A ≥ limit: multiply by −1, and the sign flips.
•  A lower bound? Take it away: $Y = y - 1$. An equality? Write it as two limits.
•  Any negative right-hand side? Pivot in that row on a negative entry, so every right-hand side ends positive. Then carry on as usual.

•  Multiplying a ≥ limit by −1 also flips the sign.
•  A negative right-hand side comes first, even if the bottom row has no negatives.
•  After the first pivot, check every right-hand side is positive before carrying on.
•  A minimise gives $P = -C$: the answer is $C = -P$, so the minimum is 8, not −8.
